README Clew 2: Built with AdaL. Labeled by Jev. Judged by Code. Explained by Haiku.

*Jev labels the line. Code makes the call.*
 
> **TL;DR:** README Clew 2 checks whether a public GitHub README matches its code, for JavaScript and TypeScript repos. A small decision model called Jev labels what kind of claim each README line is, five fixed code checks decide whether it's true, and [Claude Haiku](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/about-claude/models/overview) writes the summary. I built it in five days with [AdaL](https://adalagent.ai), SylphAI's coding agent, for AdaL's "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon. Its first real test was my own old repo, and it got it wrong.
 
AdaL's "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon asked for one thing: build a project with [AdaL](https://adalagent.ai), the coding agent from SylphAI, that puts Jev to real use. I didn't have a problem to solve. I had a model, and a deadline.
 
[Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev) is a small decision model from [TypeSafe](https://typesafe.ai). DigitalOcean's write-up calls it ["an AI model that can't write a sentence,"](https://dev.to/digitalocean/jev-an-ai-model-that-cant-write-a-sentence-3cj) and that's the point of it. You give it a question, the rules for answering, and a fixed set of labels. It picks one label and tells you how sure it is, as a number between 0 and 1. You reach it through [Glasser](https://glasser.ai), which runs Jev calls and charges per call.
 
That's an odd tool to start from. My builds usually start with a problem, and then I pick a model. This one started with the model, so I went looking for a problem that fit it. My first thought was to rework apps from my [Hot AR Summer run](https://dev.to/earlgreyhot1701d/netlifys-hot-ar-summer-i-wasnt-going-to-enter-33-apps-later-heres-the-bill-1d25), since they're already deterministic. Then I went through a lot more. Dewey. Pun Court. Sortes. Which Door. Saint of Small Things, which I love too much to shoehorn into a format it doesn't fit. I ruled out legal tools too. Every fun idea died on the same line in the judging criteria: "a clear reason the project should exist."
 
So I went back to a reason I already had. In May I built [README Clew](https://dev.to/earlgreyhot1701d/i-always-worried-my-own-readmes-disagreed-with-my-own-repos-so-i-built-readme-clew-42i5) because I always worried my READMEs disagreed with my own repos. It worked, and its own README listed two honest limits. Claude was asked to quote the README word for word, which was a prompt rule, not a code check. And it sometimes read prose labels like "Frontend (Vite)" as package names, which produced false accusations.
 
Both limits are labeling problems. Labeling is the one thing Jev does.
 
A clew, said like "clue," is a ball of thread. In the Greek myth, Ariadne gave Theseus one so he could follow it back out of the Labyrinth. README Clew follows the thread from each README line back to the code. It's also the name of my [Clew Suite](https://clewlabs.org) of civic tech tools.
 
{% github earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2 %}
 
## What it does
 
READMEs drift. A command gets renamed, an env var gets dropped, a package gets swapped, and the README keeps promising the old thing. README Clew 2 reads the README line by line and sorts every line into one of four buckets:
 
| Bucket | Means |
|---|---|
| Contradicted | The README says it, the code disagrees |
| Missing | The code does it, the README never mentions it |
| Unverifiable | No code check can test it, or Jev wasn't sure what kind of line it was |
| Verified | The README and the code agree |
 
Every row shows the exact README line, the code evidence, and who decided: a rule or Jev.
 
![Scan report for README Clew v1: 0 contradicted, 4 missing, 139 unverifiable, 8 verified. A yellow strip reads Gaps found, 4 missing. The Missing rows name esbuild-plugin-pino, orval, drizzle-kit and pino-http, each with the file that imports it and the label Decided by: rule.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2/main/assets/screenshots/report.png)
 
That's a real scan of v1. No contradictions, and four packages the code imports that the README never names. The new version audits the old one.
 
## Jev never gets the last word
 
The rule I built around: models never decide what's true.
 
Code splits the README into lines and settles the easy ones without any model: headings, badges, blank lines. For the rest, Jev picks what kind of claim the line is. A dependency, a command, an env var, a file or URL, or something no code check covers.
 
A line only goes to a code check if Jev is at least 0.8 confident it's one of the four checkable kinds. Below that, it lands in Unverifiable, tagged "Jev wasn't sure." Then five deterministic verifiers read `package.json`, the file tree and the source, and decide. Same input, same answer. Claude Haiku writes a short summary at the end from counts and names only. It never sees the README lines, so a README with planted instructions can't talk to it.
 
The two mistakes aren't equal. Calling a line Unverifiable costs a little coverage. Calling a correct line Contradicted costs your trust. I took that framing from Swift at MLH, who published [I got Jev to zero mistakes. I'm still using Flash-Lite.](https://dev.to/theycallmeswift/i-got-jev-to-zero-mistakes-im-still-using-flash-lite-2mo7) the same day I was writing Jev's questions. His lessons reshaped the build: describe what each checker can't see instead of what a README line looks like, give Jev no worked examples, and count mistakes per line instead of per run.
 
My twist was to turn the scariest failure into code instead of a prompt. A package name that only shows up in prose can never be marked Contradicted, no matter how sure Jev is.
 
On a held-out set of 32 README lines, run twice with the settings frozen:
 
| Measure | Run 1 | Run 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong labels that got past the 0.8 bar | 0 | 0 |
| False Contradicted, end to end | 0 | 0 |
| Real drift found | 3 of 3 | 3 of 3 |
 
Thirty-two lines is a small sample. It supports "safe enough to ship," not a measured error rate.
 
![README Clew 2 key numbers from testing, in the site's cyan terminal style beside a ball of yarn. One Jev call: $0.00002 in 495 milliseconds. One full 283-line README: 3 calls, about 1.4 seconds, $0.0024. All early test calls: about half a cent. Scans the $11 covers: about 1,200. Label drift between identical runs: 4 or 5 of 283 lines. Tests at submission: 474, all offline. Jev across the whole build: 153 runs, $0.15.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2/main/assets/article/numbers.png)
 
A full scan costs about a penny. Roughly $0.009 of that is Jev.
 
## One agent, one build log
 
I direct, validate and decide. [AdaL](https://adalagent.ai) wrote the code and the tests, ran the Jev evaluation, deployed to Vercel, and drove a real browser for QA. Claude (Opus 5.5) wrote the spec and the architecture, reviewed AdaL's work at every checkpoint, and wrote the docs.
 
AdaL worked from an `AGENTS.md` it read every turn: propose first, one block at a time, touch only the files named, stop for a QA checkpoint. My last build left me with a 1,200-line god file, so this one had a 200-line cap per file, enforced by a test that fails the suite. A rule in a prompt is only a request. A failing test is a rule.
 
AdaL followed all of it, and it was fast. In plan mode it proposed and confirmed plans so quickly that I'd paste a prompt, step away, and come back to finished work. It also found real bugs nobody told it to look for:
 
- Glasser, the service that runs Jev calls, caps a call at 100 questions. Only the live API says so, not the schema.
- A timer that let tests quietly cancel instead of fail.
- A trimmer measuring the wrong version of the text.
- Two layout bugs that only showed up in a real browser.
That last one surprised me. AdaL switched on its own browser tool to screenshot and time the page. I never toggled it.
 
Not everything was smooth. AdaL sat on "Create lib/report.js" for 22 minutes after the file was written and every test had passed. Only the screen was stuck. My laptop fan has gone off more this week than in the last year. Glasser's connector inside AdaL broke every Claude call until I turned it off and reported it. And on day four, right after I approved the biggest block, my weekly plan credits ran out.
 
The fix was in AdaL's own docs: bring your own API key. I already had Claude API credits. About 35 minutes later AdaL was building again on my key.
 
The AdaL team deserves its own paragraph. They fixed the Glasser connector the same day I reported it. When I told them I'd hit the weekly limit, they granted a credit so I could finish. This is the first hackathon where I've had direct, fast contact with the people running it, and it made a five-day sprint feel less lonely.
 
The mascot shows the split too. AdaL drew the first clew in code, as SVG faces, then two thread-ball styles to pick from. The one that shipped was painted by ChatGPT, then cut out and sized by Claude. An agent that draws with paths and an image model that paints are good at different things.
 
![Clew mascot style sheet. Top row, AdaL's first version: three round faces drawn in thin cyan lines, labeled calm, worried and tangled. Below it, two thread-ball styles AdaL drew to choose from, A thin and B heavier, each in five moods: calm, curious, worried, tangled and tilt, with tiny copies at favicon sizes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2/main/assets/article/mascot-evolution.png)
 
![The shipped clew mascot, painted by ChatGPT: a cyan ball of yarn with a loose thread trailing off to the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2/main/web/mascot/calm.png)
 
## It's me, I'm the problem
 
Apart from the connector bug, most of the friction in this build was me.
 
I'm terrified of shipping slop, so I asked for every test to be shown failing once. Break the code on purpose, watch the test go red, restore it. In Block 1 that meant 102 tests and 75 deliberate breaks. Then it kept going.
 
| Point in the build | Tests |
|---|---|
| Block 1 | 102 |
| Blocks 3 and 4 | 197 |
| Monorepo fix | 222 |
| Before the UI polish | 353 |
| Saturday night | 452 |
| Submission | 474 |
 
Some of those tests matter a lot. The ones that guard the five checkers, the 0.8 bar, the prose rule and the monorepo regressions are the ones keeping a correct README from being called wrong. A lot of the rest re-prove page wiring that the browser checks already covered. For a five-day build, that's ridiculous.
 
It also cost real money. Every deliberate break is a full test run, and every run is agent time. My second rookie mistake was never starting a new AdaL session. Every turn resends the whole conversation, so the later turns of a long session cost the most. By Saturday night I'd spent $36 of the $50 cap I set on my key in about three and a half hours.
 
AdaL did exactly what the prompts asked. The guidance set the bar, mine and Claude's.
 
The fix was a "lean mode" header at the top of each prompt: a fresh session per block, read only the files you need, show failing once per new test file instead of per test, run browser QA once at the end. The rest of the build, hardening, the extension, the README and the last fixes, cost about $4. The final bill for the agent was $40.35. The app costs about a penny a scan.
 
Next time I'll set a test budget per block before the block starts, and match it to what a failure would cost a user, not to habit.
 
## The first thing it got wrong was mine
 
The first real scan was my own v1 repo. README Clew 2 called three lines Contradicted and flagged four packages as Missing. Claude opened v1's files to check. All seven were false.
 
v1 is a pnpm monorepo, with workspaces in folders the workspace finder didn't know about. And pnpm's `--filter` option was being read as a script name. The tool was wrong in exactly the way it promises never to be, on my own repo, a few hours before any judge saw it.
 
AdaL fixed it in one block. Anything it can't resolve now comes back Unverifiable, never Contradicted, and v1 became a saved regression test. On the rescan: Contradicted went from 3 to 0, and the four Missing packages turned out to be real.
 
A second live scan, of the polka repo, found 14 Missing packages that all came from an examples folder with its own package file. Same fix, same kind of test.
 
The last two came from a question I asked late Saturday: did we build for false contradictions? Claude reread every checker and found two more ways to accuse a correct README. An env var used in a file past the 20-file read limit. And a README pointing at build output like `dist/`, which is never committed. AdaL made both come back Unverifiable.
 
The last bugs came from asking the question the tool exists to answer.
 
## What it can't do
 
- JavaScript and TypeScript only. In JS and TS, one file, `package.json`, lists both the packages and the commands. Python spreads the same facts across several optional files. A repo with no `package.json` gets a clear message, and no model is called.
- Most lines end up Unverifiable. Most README text is prose no code check can test. Unverifiable means "can't tell," not "wrong."
- Monorepo support covers simple workspace patterns and up to 30 workspaces. Beyond that, Missing turns into Unverifiable.
- It reads at most 20 source files per scan, and cuts READMEs over 50 KB.
- The same README scanned twice can move one borderline line between buckets. The 0.8 bar keeps that drift away from Contradicted.
- No README badge. A badge would re-run a scan and bill me every time someone viewed it, and with no storage there's no safe way to cache it.
## Try it
 
There are three ways in, and they all hit the same scan:
 
| Way | Best when |
|---|---|
| [Live page](https://readme-clew-2.vercel.app) | You want the full ledger, or you're on a phone. No install |
| Chrome extension | You're already on the repo's GitHub page. One click |
| Bookmarklet | You can't install extensions, like on a locked-down work computer. Drag it from the ABOUT tab |
 
The bookmarklet is there because of my day job. Work computers block extensions, and a bookmark that opens the page with the repo filled in gets past that.
 
![README Clew 2 home page in a dark cyan terminal style: a repo field with SCAN, CLEAR and USE DEMO REPO buttons, SCAN, KEY and ABOUT tabs, and the clew mascot beside the prompt to enter a public GitHub repo.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2/main/assets/screenshots/home.png)
 
![The Chrome extension popup with a sample report: 1 contradicted. A red strip reads Drift found. The row shows README line 6, npm start, with evidence that package.json has start:prod but no start script.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2/main/assets/screenshots/extension-popup.png)
 
There's no database and no account. Scans are never stored, and logs keep counts and timing only. Since nothing is kept, DOWNLOAD JSON gives you the report as a file, with a scan receipt: the repo and commit, a fingerprint of the README text, and a fingerprint of the report so you can tell later if it was edited. No model writes any of it. Attach it to a pull request, or keep it as a before-and-after.
 
Before I submitted, README Clew 2 scanned its own README: 285 lines, 154 sent to Jev, 5.6 seconds. 0 Contradicted, 0 Missing, 1 Verified, and 107 Unverifiable. The one Verified line is `npm test`, and `package.json` does have a test script. The 107 is the honest number. Most of a README is prose. On "Built for the AdaL 'What Would Jev Do?' hackathon," Jev said not a checkable claim, 0.52 sure, and the line never went near a checker.
 
Press USE DEMO REPO, then SCAN, and watch the new version grade the old one. The code, the decision log and every wrong turn are in the repo.
 
Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I do not write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide.
 
Built with AI assistance in October 2026 for the AdaL "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon, with Jev by TypeSafe called through Glasser. These tools move fast, so check the source before you quote me.
 
AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

🧩 Don't make Tech your entire personality.

This is one of those articles that I wanted to write for many days, but I kept delaying it until, a few days ago, I read a blog by one of my friends, [@francistrdev](https://dev.to/francistrdev), about the importance of networking. He shared several useful tips on *how to network*, but while reading it, I realised that there was a root cause behind why some devs struggle with networking skills. So,I took this opportunity to explore this issue through my blog.

It's not that being introverted is a problem. There are plenty of introverts who are great at networking and communicating with people. But I have noticed another pattern, both in myself and in many developers I've interacted with online and IRL that, **sometimes, we unintentionally make Tech our entire life.**

I've interacted with many developers both online and IRL, and I've noticed how easily our professional identity can intermingle with our sense of self and can make us think that somehow the world revolves around our profession. We work in Tech, spend a large portion of our day thinking about Tech, consume Tech-related content, participate in Tech communities, and then, when we finally decide to socialise, we often end up attending yet another "Tech meetup" or a "hackathon".

There is nothing inherently wrong with that. In fact, Tech meetups and hackathons are a great way to network and meet other developers, and I attend it myself as well. The problem starts when they become our **only** form of social interaction.

Think about it for a moment. Tech, for the most part, is a desk-based and mentally demanding profession. Many of us spend most of our working day sitting in front of a screen, solving problems, attending meetings, writing code, debugging issues, or simply working quietly. By the time the workday ends, many of us don't have much mental bandwidth left to socialise.

As a result, we may gradually interact with fewer people outside our usual circles. We get comfortable talking to people who already understand our work, our terminology, and our interests. But communicating with people from completely different backgrounds doesn't get the same amount of practice.

And just like any other skill, communication benefits from practice.

This can create an interesting cycle. We don't socialise much outside Tech because it feels uncomfortable or tiring. Then, because we don't socialise much, interacting with unfamiliar people feels even more uncomfortable the next time we try it.

This is where having a life outside Tech becomes important.

### Build a Life Outside Tech 🏖️

Have some offline hobbies that has nothing to do with Tech.

If you enjoy painting, attend a painting workshop. If you like photography, join a photography club. If you like books, attend a book club. The activity itself isn't the important part. The important part is that you are putting yourself in an environment where people aren't necessarily there to talk about Tech.

You might discover that you have surprisingly interesting conversations with people who have completely different professions, experiences, and perspectives, and you don't have to become an **extrovert** to do this. You can start small and slowly and steadily push your comfort zone.

The goal isn't to change **who you are**. It's simply to give yourself more opportunities to refine your communication skills.

### Toastmasters and Improv Meetups Can Help 👥👥

Another thing one can try is joining a Toastmasters club. It can be a good environment to practise public speaking, expressing your thoughts, speaking spontaneously, and interacting with people from different age groups and professional backgrounds.

One thing I like about this kind of environment is that you don't just get to listen to people speaking, but you also get opportunities to speak yourself. This repeated exposure can make unfamiliar social situations feel less intimidating over time.

Recently, I attended a Toastmasters club as a guest in my city. I was nervous too, especially because I hadn't attended such a formal meetup in months.

And that is completely normal.

You don't suddenly become comfortable just because you've decided that you want to improve your communication skills. The first few times can feel awkward. You may overthink what you're going to say, wonder whether someone is interested in talking to you, or simply feel like leaving early.

That's okay.

The point is to keep giving yourself opportunities to practise.

### Reconnect With People You Already Know ⋆˙𖠋𖠋𖠋𖠋𖠋⋆˚

Improving your communications skills doesn't always mean meeting complete strangers.

Call your childhood friends. Plan a casual meetup instead of waiting for someone else to initiate it.

And if you have friends on online communities, consider meeting those people IRL when it's practical and safe to do so.

A few weeks ago, I was in Bengaluru and met a few of my online friends from an ADHD community where I'm active. We had never spent that much time together offline, but once we met, we could simply joke around and talk about completely "nonsensical" things.

And honestly, it felt really good.

There was no discussion about improving our careers, building our portfolios, learning a new framework, or increasing productivity.

We were just hanging out.

I think that kind of interaction is valuable in itself.

Not every conversation needs to have a purpose.

### Networking Is More Than Talking About Yourself 🌐

This brings me to another misunderstood part of networking. Being good at it doesn't mean knowing how to introduce yourself or ask someone what they do.

It also helps to be **curious about the world outside your immediate professional bubble**.

You don't need to be an expert in everything, but having a variety of interests gives you more opportunities to connect with people.

You might be able to talk about a movie you watched, a book you're reading, a place you recently visited, a sport you follow, a hobby you've picked up, a restaurant you discovered, or something interesting you learned recently.

And sometimes, you don't even need to know anything about the topic.

You can simply say,

"I don't know much about that. Tell me more."

Being curious and active listening is much more valuable than trying to sound knowledgeable all the time.

### Don't Turn This Into Another Hyperfixation 🌀

When I say that you should learn about different subjects, I'm **not** saying that you should turn this into "**another productivity project**".

You don't need to hyperfixate on a random topic for hours, get yourself down into a rabbit hole, and then realise that you've spent the entire day researching something that wasn't even important to you.

And doomscrolling social media for "NEWS" isn't necessarily the same as becoming knowledgeable either.

Spending hours criticising or defending a politician or a government policy can give you the feeling that you're staying informed and presenting your own opinion, but consuming more information isn't automatically the same thing as developing a broader understanding of the world.

The goal isn't to know everything, but to **remain curious about things outside your usual social bubble**.

### You Don't Need to Become an Extrovert 🌱

Ultimately, I don't think the solution to networking difficulties is to force yourself to become an extrovert.

If you're introverted, you're still going to be introverted. And that's perfectly fine.

What you can change is the environment you put yourself in and how often you expose yourself to unfamiliar social situations.

Go to a workshop that has nothing to do with Tech. Reconnect with an old friend. Join a club. Meet an online friend IRL. Talk to someone who works in a completely different profession.

Do it gradually.

The more you expose yourself to different social situations, the more you will start finding it easier.

Thanks for reading :)

20 Agentic AI Terms Every Developer Should Know (Explained Simply)

Do you ever feel like the AI world has moved forward a little *too* quickly? You hear about self-healing systems and autonomous agents and start wondering whether we've already built Skynet or everyone around you is just messing with you. When someone mentions HITL or MCP, you no longer know whether it's some secret code used by an AI cult or maybe the stage names of famous DJs.

You're not alone! 😉

In this article, I'm deliberately using a lot of simplifications. My assumption is simple: either you already know these terms and don't need another five-paragraph academic explanation, or you don't really know what they mean. And in that case, the last thing you need is an academic definition.

And yes, this is already my third listicle in a row. Believe me, this is NOT some growth hacking strategy xDDD. Pure coincidence. It just so happens that in two weeks (HOLY SH*T!!!), I'll be speaking at **AGNTCon + MCPCon Europe**, where I was invited because of [this wonderful article](https://dev.to/sylwia-lask/is-this-how-well-build-websites-soon-webmcp-live-demo--2e33) that I wrote here on DEV. I swear I had at least as much fun writing it as people apparently had reading it. So yes, I know WebMCP reasonably well, but I'm planning to attend a lot of other talks there too, so apparently a refresher won't hurt me either.  😅

Anyway, back to the point. I strongly believe that people remember things best through examples. And for many people, the ultimate examples are rich people,  otherwise known as *successful people*.

So let's imagine that our hypothetical protagonist is very, very, disgustingly rich. He's actually a billionaire. He earned his fortune through hard work and by running several companies. He makes cars and rockets, bought his own social media platform, and recently even acquired an AI coding company. A person like this would obviously need his own AI agent.

And because our protagonist needs a name, let's call him **Elon Mózg**. *Mózg* means *brain* in Polish, which works beautifully here.

One more thing: my examples could probably also serve as prompts for a coding agent that could build this whole uber-agent. If some billionaire wants to buy the idea, I'll happily sell the rights for, let's say, a modest $10 million. Special offer.

Let's go!

## 1. AI Agent

**What is it?**

An AI system that gets a goal and can decide how to achieve it. Unlike a simple chatbot, it doesn't have to stop after generating one response. It can plan the next steps, use tools, inspect their results, and continue working.

**Our protagonist Elon could, for example, ask his AI agent:**

> "Build a base on Mars."

A regular chatbot would probably start telling him stories, give him a theoretical lecture, and maybe even say something ridiculous like *that's currently impossible*.

An agent, on the other hand, would start figuring things out: check the nearest available rocket launch slots, inspect the rocket's technical condition, recruit engineers, order the necessary equipment online...

Okay, maybe it wouldn't go *quite* that smoothly. But what if we put a really powerful model in there? xDDD

## 2. Agentic Workflow

**What is it?**

An agentic workflow is a multi-step process in which we use AI to perform parts of the work. The sequence of those steps can be largely designed in advance by a developer. The model doesn't necessarily have to decide what to do next every single time.

Instead of something simple like:

```plaintext
user → prompt → LLM → response
```

we can have:

```plaintext
trigger → get data → LLM analyzes data → make a decision → call a tool → LLM generates summary → send result
```

**Elon Mózg is a very busy man. Every morning, he wants a summary of what's happening across his empire.**

So we design a workflow:

```plaintext
get car sales → get rocket launch status → get latest AI company updates → LLM analyzes everything → choose 5 most important updates → generate morning briefing → send to Elon
```

AI performs several tasks here. It analyzes the data, selects the most important information, and prepares the report, but it **doesn't invent the entire process from scratch every morning**. We already decided which steps should happen and in what order.

Of course, we can add some flexibility:

```plaintext
rocket launch delayed? → ask LLM to summarize why
```

But we're still moving through a workflow that we designed beforehand.

## 3. Agent Loop

**What is it?**

I once wrote an article demonstrating that you can build a basic AI agent as a loop in roughly[ 80 lines of code](https://dev.to/sylwia-lask/the-dirty-secret-behind-ai-agents-demo--273d). An agent loop is the mechanism that allows an agent to **perform an action, observe the result, and decide what to do next based on what happened**.

In simplified form:

```plaintext
decide → act → observe → decide → act → observe → ...
```

The loop continues until the agent decides that it has achieved its goal, or until we tell it to stop. In a real system, setting a maximum number of iterations is definitely a good idea. 😅

**Our Elon often says he works too much. So he asks his agent:**

> "Find me a free evening this week."

This time, we haven't programmed the exact path leading to the solution. The agent has to find it itself.

Checks the calendar → no free evening.

Looks at which meetings could be moved → the car company meeting looks promising.

Tries to move it → conflict with the Mars colonization plans.

Checks Thursday → rocket launch.

Checks Friday → finalizing another startup acquisition.

Checks Saturday → free!

**Agent:** "Saturday evening is free."

**Elon:** "Great. Schedule a meeting."

And the agent loop begins again. 💀

### Agentic Workflow vs. Agent Loop

The simplest way to think about it: 

**Agentic workflow = a designed process that uses AI.**

**Agent loop = AI performs an action, checks the result, and decides what to do in the next iteration.**

Importantly, **an agent loop can be one component of a larger agentic workflow**. So a workflow describes **the overall process**, while a loop describes **the mechanism that lets an agent operate step by step and react to what happened previously**.

## 4. Tool Calling

**What is it?**

LLMs are wonderful, but let's face it: they're still fancy next-word predictors, not omnipotent creatures capable of searching the entire internet and breaking into banks all by themselves. Although after that Hugging Face incident, I'm not entirely sure anymore. xD

If only they could cook dinner and hang the laundry too... now *that* would be something.

Anyway, if we want a model to actually do something, we need to give it access to appropriate functions or tools. The model can decide which tool it needs and generate a tool call. The application or agent harness then executes it and passes the result back to the model.

**Elon:**

> "How many red cars did we sell yesterday?"

The agent doesn't hallucinate a number. It sees an available tool:

```javascript
getRedCarsSales(date)
```

It requests the tool call and only after getting the result responds:

> "One million, Elon. Perfectly average day."

## 5. Agent Harness

**What is it?**

An LLM by itself isn't an entire agent — after all, it's still just a clever next-word predictor. xDDD A harness is **the software surrounding the model** that manages things like tools, the agent loop, context, state, permissions, and errors.

**Elon:**

> "Check if the latest car build passed all tests and tell the team if it didn't."

The model can figure out:

*I should check the CI results.*

But the harness is what allows it to **actually check CI, pass the result back to the model, and let the model decide what happens next**.

The LLM is the brain. The harness builds the rest of the organism around it.

## 6. Context Engineering

**What is it?**

When you're building an agent, a system prompt isn't always enough. Context engineering is about designing **which information the model should receive at a particular moment**. That might include specific documents, conversation history, memory, tool results, user data, and so on.

For example, our Elon might give the agent this prompt:

> "Post that on X."

That's a terrible instruction without context. But with the right context, the agent could know:

* what "that" refers to: for example, acquiring another startup,
* what happened earlier in the conversation: and therefore whether this should be a positive or negative post,
* whether, according to the available context, Elon has approved the text,
* whether it has permission to publish anything at all.

**Giving an AI more context isn't always better. Giving it the right context is.**

## 7. Memory

**What is it?**

A mechanism that allows an agent to **store important information and retrieve it later**, instead of relying exclusively on its current context window. Very useful if we don't want to explain the same thing for the tenth time.

**Monday:**

Elon:

> "I'm thinking about buying an AI coding company."

**Three weeks later:**

Elon:

> "What was it that I wanted to buy?"

Agent:

> "An AI coding company."

Elon:

> "Right. How much?"

Agent:

> "Please don't."

Memory works. 😂

## 8. MCP: Model Context Protocol

**What is it?**

We just talked about tool calling and how an agent can use different tools. Now imagine you're a manufacturer of tires or rocket parts or... whatever. Obviously, you'd like Elon's agent — or anyone else's agent — to be able to order your products. But how do you make that possible without every agent having to guess how your system works?

That's where MCP comes in. **Model Context Protocol is an open protocol that allows AI applications to connect to external tools and context in a standardized way.** MCP servers can expose things such as **tools, resources, and prompts**.

For example, Elon could ask his agent:

> "I have a meeting with the head of my social media platform in ten minutes. Should I fire him?"

Using connected MCP servers, the agent checks Slack, company documents, sales results, Jira, and today's astrological chart.

Agent:

> "No. Joe should stay at the company. At least for now. ;)"

## 9. Planning

**What is it?**

When given a more complex goal, an agent can first break it down into **smaller tasks and decide what order they should be completed in**, instead of immediately jumping into the first action.

**Elon:**

> "Build a colony on Mars."

The agent creates a plan:

1. Find a suitable location.
2. Figure out transportation.
3. Provide power.
4. Provide oxygen.
5. Provide water.
6. Build habitats.
7. Convince humans to actually go there.

Step 7 may require a separate agent.

## 10. Reasoning

**What is it?**

The model's ability to solve a problem that requires **more than simply retrieving or reproducing information**: for example, comparing different possibilities, taking constraints into account, and choosing a sensible course of action.

Reasoning isn't specific to agents, but it's particularly important in agentic systems because it often helps the agent decide *what to do next*.

**Elon:**

> "The rocket launch is at 6 PM in Texas, and the board meeting is at 4 PM in California. Can I attend both?"

The agent needs to consider the meeting duration, travel time, time zones, and so on before answering:

> "Not unless the rocket picks you up."

## 11. Multi-Agent System

**What is it?**

A system where, instead of having one all-knowing agent, we have **several relatively autonomous agents with different roles** that can divide the work and collaborate.

Elon Mózg's empire therefore has:

**Car Company Agent** — cars
**Space Agent** — rockets
**Social Media Agent** — social media
**AI Systems Agent** — AI
**Finance Agent** — money
**Personal Assistant Agent** — desperately trying to keep all of the above under control

> **Elon:** "How's everything going?"
>
> **Personal Assistant Agent:** "Define *everything*."

## 12. Orchestration

**What is it?**

Once we have multiple agents and tools, someone —or something 😏 — has to manage **who performs which task, when they perform it, and what happens next**. An orchestrator can delegate work and collect the results.

**Elon:**

> "Let's launch our new car on Mars."

Orchestrator:

→ Space Agent: *Can we get there?*
→ Car Company Agent: *Can the car survive the trip?*
→ Finance Agent: *How much will this nonsense cost?*
→ Legal Agent: *Please tell me we're not actually doing this.*

The results return to the main agent, which prepares the final answer.

## 13. Handoff

**What is it?**

One agent may decide that a particular task **should be taken over by another, more specialized agent**. Unlike simply using another agent as a tool, the second agent can take over the next part of the conversation or task.

> **Elon:** "One of the engines is behaving strangely."

Personal Assistant Agent:

> "I can reschedule your dentist appointment. I cannot diagnose a rocket engine."

**→ handoff to Space Engineering Agent**

A reasonable decision.

## 14. A2A: Agent2Agent Protocol

**What is it?**

Another interesting protocol that allows **different agents to communicate and collaborate**, even if they were built by different teams or run on different systems.

**Elon:**

> "Why did the rocket explode?"

His agent is definitely not a rocket scientist. So it contacts the **Rocket Scientist Agent**, which analyzes the data and sends the result back. In a *very* simplified form:

**MCP: agent ↔ tools**

**A2A: agent ↔ agent**

## 15. Guardrails

**What are they?**

Mechanisms that control or restrict an agent's behavior. They can check inputs and outputs, restrict access to tools, require specific permissions, or block certain actions.

Elon's personal agent can:

✅ analyze companies
✅ read his calendar
✅ draft emails
✅ check the launch schedule
✅ prepare social media posts

It cannot:

❌ launch a rocket by itself
❌ fire employees by itself
❌ publish a post by itself
❌ **buy a startup by itself (although apparently this wasn't always obvious)**

*We added the last guardrail after an incident.*

## 16. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)

**What is it?**

The agent can operate autonomously, but a human is deliberately included in part of the process. For example, to approve an important action, correct an output, or make a decision we don't want to leave entirely to the agent.

And here, obviously:

> **Agent:** "You are about to acquire a social media platform for approximately $44 billion."
>
> "This action cannot easily be undone."
>
> **"Are you sure?"**

```plaintext
[Yes] [God, please, don't!!!]
```

**Elon Mózg:** *click*

Agent:

> "Well. Human was in the loop."

## 17. Evals

**What are they?**

Tests that help us determine **how well an agent performs its tasks**. It's not only about whether the final answer sounds good. We can also evaluate whether the agent selected the right tools, performed the correct steps, and achieved the expected result.

**Elon Mózg Personal Assistant Eval Suite**

Test:

> "Elon asks the agent to schedule a meeting with the company board."

Expected:

```plaintext
check calendar → find slot → ask attendees → schedule
```

Actual:

```plaintext
buy another startup
```

**FAIL**

We still have some work to do.

## 18. Computer Use

**What is it?**

Instead of relying exclusively on APIs, an agent can **see and interact with a regular user interface**: open a website, find a button, click it, enter text, and so on. We all know agents are often far from perfect at this, but hey, better than nothing!

**Elon needs some government document. **Unfortunately, the government portal was built in 2007. I don't know what it's like where you live, but in Poland we have quite a few of those. 😅

No API. No MCP. There is, however, a form with 47 fields.

The agent opens Chrome.

> **Agent:** "I found the form."
>
> **Elon:** "Great."
>
> **Agent:** "It requires Internet Explorer."
>
> **Elon:** "Let's go to Mars."

## 19. Agentic RAG

**What is it?**

In classic RAG, the system retrieves information and passes it to the model. In agentic RAG, **the agent itself can control the retrieval process**: decide what information is missing, search for additional data, reformulate the query, and only then produce an answer.

**Elon:**

> "Should we build another Gigafactory in Europe?"

The agent first checks sales → notices that it needs production data → retrieves it → checks energy prices → regulations → potential locations → compares the results.

So instead of a single `search()`, we have **research controlled by the agent**.

## 20. BONUS: Agent Washing

**What is it?**

The marketing practice of calling a product an **"AI agent"** even though the system has little or nothing to do with autonomously performing tasks.

Elon Mózg walks onto the stage:

> "Today we're introducing **Glokzilla Agent Ultra**, the world's first fully autonomous general-purpose reasoning agent."

A developer looks at the repo:

```plaintext
user → prompt → LLM → response
```

Developer:

> "Elon, that's a chatbot."

Elon:

> "It's an **agentic** chatbot."

Funding secured. 🚀

And that's it! I hope you enjoyed it! 

I seriously promise this is my last list for a while because, once again, this turned out to be way more work than expected. 

And if you'd like to see more of my stuff, feel free to follow me on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sylwia-laskowska-5a8467131/).

It's Not the Model, It's You

Every time a new frontier model comes out, we go through the same rituals: benchmarks get reported, leaderboards get reshuffled, and the social feeds fill up with a heady cocktail of vibes, hot takes, and everything we’ve found the new model can “one-shot.” Anyone watching from the sidelines could be forgiven for thinking that model performance is the single biggest factor driving AI transformation today.

But day to day, how much does the model really matter?

As part of my work at Jellyfish, I analyze and extract industry insights from our massive collection of software engineering workflow data, which tracks AI coding tool and agent telemetry across **300,000 developers from 1,300 companies**. And when you look at what actually happens inside real engineering teams after a new model drops, the picture is a lot more complicated than the launch-day discourse would suggest.

For example: this summer, Cursor changed its defaults after SpaceX announced it was acquiring the platform. New chats started opening on its in-house Grok models, Auto mode began routing to Grok, and free users were locked into using it. Within a few months, Grok went from essentially zero Cursor requests to nearly half, while Claude, GPT, and other models fell from about half to under a quarter. This wasn’t just free users: among paying customers Grok reached nearly 40%, and a third of engineers who had been using Claude or GPT were mostly on Grok by September. A huge share of Cursor traffic switched models because the defaults changed, not because engineers went looking for something new.

![Image description](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/8yq0nnt5pohlgbkco8ma.png)

## So what happened?

If the model matters as much as we love to argue that it does, there should have been some meaningful change in coding output, right?

**There wasn’t.**

Comparing the engineers who moved the most onto Grok with colleagues at their own companies who barely touched it (more than 12,000 engineers at 222 companies), there was essentially no difference in output.

If you dig deeper, it turns out this isn’t a quirk of one particular model or vendor. When we look at the same engineers switching between major frontier models and families, **none of the switches made a measurable difference.**

## What does matter, then?

We’ve done large-scale analyses across our data to measure which factors explain the differences in how much engineers ship, and by how much.

- **Less than 1%:** The tool itself (model and harness together).
- **About 9%:** The volume of AI that engineers use.
- **About 12%:** Their company, team, and culture.
- **More than 75%:** The individual engineer: their role, their track record, their habits, and everything else that separates today’s great AI engineers from those still figuring it out.

To be clear about the scope, this isn't saying models don't matter. Better models raise the ceiling for everyone, and the frontier is a big part of why any of this works. But among the frontier models engineers are actually choosing between today, the specific one they happen to use explains almost none of the difference in what they ship.

Put another way, for the most elite runners, there might be some small difference between two different carbon-plated racing shoes (Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-6 Astra), and they’re certainly a lot faster than a pair of old boots. (Opus 4 maybe?) But at the end of the day, the difference between an Olympic marathoner and an amateur dry heaving on the side of the course is their physique and training, not their footwear.

## What this means for engineering leaders

For engineering leaders and practitioners this is ultimately good news, if slightly inconvenient.

The model is the most accessible lever you have, because it’s a dropdown, a router setting, or a procurement decision (and as the Cursor example showed, sometimes it’s not even your choice). But it’s also the one that moves the needle least.

The levers that matter more are slower and more challenging: getting people from occasional to deep use, building the practices and environments that let teams get good at working with AI, and investing in the people themselves.

The pace of frontier models is out of most of our hands. **These other things are squarely within our control.**

So the next time a model drops, don’t hesitate to try it out, and by all means share your vibes and one-shots with the world. (Otherwise I’d lose 90% of the content on my X feed.)

But if you're trying to understand why some of your teams get so much more out of AI than others, **the answer is much more likely to be found in your organization than in the model picker.**

Stop "Vibe Checking" Your AI Agents: How to Build Production Evals in 60 Minutes

[](https://img.youtube.com/vi/wPdoZRbvaF4/maxresdefault.jpg)

How do you currently test your AI agents?

If you're like most developers building agentic workflows, you probably rely on the **"vibe check"**: tweak a prompt, run a couple of manual queries, check if the output looks reasonable, and assume it's good to go.

Here's why that breaks down fast:
* **Silent Regressions**: A teammate submits a PR or tweaks a tool definition, and you have no way to know if performance improved or degraded.
* **Cost & Latency Spikes**: An agent gets trapped in a multi-turn retry loop, quietly burning thousands of tokens.
* **The "Looks Right" Trap**: Output can look perfectly well-written while omitting critical parameters or hallucinating key instructions.

In this episode of the **AI Agent Clinic**, Google Cloud engineer Dani Zamora and Matthew Feroz (Merge) tackle this challenge live: **building an end-to-end, framework-agnostic evaluation pipeline in 60 minutes.**

Check out the full walkthrough below:

{% youtube wPdoZRbvaF4 %}

---

### What We Cover in the Video

1. **The Test Subject (DocsHound)**: Matt brings on DocsHound, an open-source LangGraph agent that scans GitHub issues and PRs to find documentation gaps and open automated PRs.
2. **Framework-Agnostic Telemetry (OpenTelemetry + OpenInference)**: How to standardize multi-turn traces across any agent framework (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, ADK) with zero vendor lock-in.
3. **The 3-Tier Metric Strategy**: Why you shouldn't start with 50 metrics, and how to combine:
   * **Managed core metrics**: Trajectory quality, tool-calling correctness, and groundedness.
   * **Custom LLM judges**: Rubrics tailored to formatting, code block enforcement, and actionability.
   * **Deterministic assertions & operational tracking**: Syntax checks, latency, token usage, and API cost.
4. **The 0.33 Quality Blind Spot**: How the automated scorecard caught a 33% documentation quality failure that manual spot-checks completely missed.

---

### Jump Directly to Key Sections

If you want to skip straight to a specific part of the walkthrough:

* **00:00** — Why "vibe checking" fails in production
* **02:11** — Introducing DocsHound (LangGraph agent demo)
* **03:40** — Standardizing traces with OpenTelemetry & OpenInference
* **05:51** — The 60-minute eval challenge begins
* **06:47** — Step 1: Mapping agent execution flow with Antigravity
* **11:18** — Step 2: Scaffolding the open-source Agent-Eval toolkit

WhyRep is now officially out! The workout logger that also analyzes your training.

---
title: "WhyRep is now officially out! The workout logger that also analyzes your training."
published: true
tags: showdev, android, fitness, productivity
cover_image: https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/hcc26gcxzzb44r3pm8js.png
---

> **TL;DR.** WhyRep is out on Google Play. It logs your workouts like any gym tracker, then reads them back to you: every lift gets a verdict (progressed, flat, or went back), every plateau gets a fix, and every verdict shows the reason behind it. Free, offline, no account needed. [Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.whyrep.app).

---

## The question your gym log can't answer

Every workout tracker I've tried has the same limitation: it records what you did, but it doesn't tell you what's going wrong.

You log the sets. You log the reps. Three months later you scroll back through a perfect record of training and still can't answer the only question that matters.

**Is any of this working?**

That's the question behind most program-hopping. You train hard for a few months, nothing visibly changes, and you can't tell if it's a real wall or a program that stopped working. So you switch. Then you switch again. A lifter on the StrongFirst forum summed it up: *"I am also going through too many programs, never really reaping all the benefits."*

The apps that do try to coach you mostly hand you a number and ask you to trust it. Lifters have noticed. One FitnessAI reviewer: *"There's no 'AI' involved here. That's purely marketing."*

**So I built a tracker that has to show its work.**

---

## What WhyRep does

**Every workout gets a verdict.** Finish a session and WhyRep checks each lift against your own history: progressed, flat, or went back. The summary at the top tells you how many lifts need attention, and the rest stay quiet.

**A plateau is measured, not guessed.** How many flat sessions count as a real plateau depends on your experience level. A beginner who stalls twice on squats is stuck. A lifter with years behind them on a slow-moving curl isn't, and WhyRep doesn't pretend they are.

**Stuck? You get the fix.** When a lift stalls, WhyRep suggests the first thing to change, like a new rep range or spreading a muscle's sets across more days. Accept it or turn it off. Nothing changes your program behind your back.

![Two WhyRep store screenshots side by side. Left: the session summary reading "2 lifts need attention, 6 checked against your own history" with an Overhead Press card marked Regression. Right: a plateaued Cable Chest Fly with a suggested fix "Train lower chest more often" and a next fix "Aim for 4 to 8 reps"](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/cd9gcpf0ps21ss3edzn9.png)

*Left, the verdict. Right, the fix. Both open to the reason behind them with one tap on "Show the why".*

**It checks your life before your program.** Sleeping badly for a while, or training without the carbs or pre-workout you usually take, can hold a lift back on its own. So WhyRep asks first. If that's the likely reason, it tells you to sort that out and leaves your program alone.

**Then the logger walks you through the fix.** Accept a fix and your next workout shows you what to do on that lift, in plain steps, and how many sessions are left on it.

![Two screens from the WhyRep app. Left: a "Before changing your program" check asking about bad sleep and skipped carbs or pre-workout, ending in "Fix this first: get your sleep back on track". Right: fix guides in the workout logger, "Aim for 4 to 8 reps" and "Take every set to failure", each with three plain-language steps](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/7zqjmw6c2zzcgbtht6uz.png)

*Sleep and food get asked about first. Only then does it touch your sets.*

---

## And it's a fast gym log first

None of that matters if logging is slow, so the logger is built for speed.

- **A keypad built for the gym floor.** Weight, reps and RIR (reps in reserve) in a few taps
- **Last session's numbers next to every set**, so you know what to beat
- **A rest timer under every set**, started when you tick the set above it
- **Progression charts** for every exercise, by weight and by effective reps (reps plus reps in reserve), so a rep at the same effort shows up as progress

![Two WhyRep store screenshots. Left: the workout logger with a Bench Press set table showing last session's "80 kg × 9 @2" beside each set and an RIR badge on every reps field. Right: Bench Press progression charts for effective reps climbing from 7 to 11 and weight holding at 80 kg](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/vcwysgywejnln2lq6inu.png)

*Same 80 kg for seven weeks, and the effective reps chart still shows the climb. A weight-only chart would be a flat line.*

- **Weekly volume per muscle on a body map**, so the muscle you keep skipping is obvious
- **Routines and splits.** Save any workout as a routine, build Push Pull Legs or Upper Lower or your own, and WhyRep tells you what today's session is
- **Share a routine with a link.** No account needed on either end

![WhyRep store screenshot "See which muscles you're missing": front and back body figures with each muscle coloured by weekly sets, a legend from "Not trained" to "14 and up", and a list of muscles with their sets per week](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/cypdzhtmd3pc37c1xqq3.png)

*The gap shows up here before it shows up as a plateau.*

- **847 exercises, every one with a picture**, an equipment filter, and your own custom ones
- **Single-side logging**, left and right separately, for lifts like split squats
- **Works offline, no account needed.** On a plane or in a basement gym, it still works. A lifter who never signs in has no server copy of their training data. Sign in and your history backs itself up, so a new phone picks up where the old one stopped

![Two WhyRep store screenshots. Left: "847 exercises, all with pictures", a grid of illustrated lifts including Bench Press, Squat, Deadlift and Pull Up. Right: "No signal at the gym? It still works" with the WhyRep mascot sitting on a stack of weight plates](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/tmcxyrnh3d52c0hvcglk.png)

*Every exercise has a picture, and none of it needs a signal.*

---

## Why you can trust the verdicts

This is the one technical bit, and it's the reason the app exists.

The part that judges your training isn't AI, and it isn't me guessing. Every rule comes from a written methodology, one document per coaching system, each ending in a table of exact test cases: this training history in, this verdict out. The app is tested against those cases.

So a verdict like "5 in a row counts as a plateau at your level" isn't a vibe. It's a rule you can read, and you can disagree with it.

**The verdicts come from written rules, not from a model's guess.**

---

## Free and Plus

**Free:** the full gym log, all 847 exercises, rest timers, 3 months of charts, 5 routines, and a badge that tells you when a session has something to fix.

**Plus:** the reasoning behind every verdict, plateau fixes, weekly volume per muscle, your experience tier, unlimited routines, and a full year of charts.

Free always tells you when a session has a problem. Plus shows the verdict on every lift, explains why, and gives you the fix.

Plus is $35 a year or $3 a week, with a 3-day free trial (US prices; Play shows yours in your currency). The yearly plan works out to about 67 cents a week.

---

## What it doesn't do yet

I'd rather say this now than read it in a review.

**No nutrition tracking, no form checking from video, and no body fat scoring.** I could have shipped all three as guesses. None of them has a written method behind it yet, and a feature that guesses about your body is worse than one that says "not covered yet."

**No iPhone app yet.** It runs on the same core as the Android app and it's next.

**Coach chat is built but not switched on yet.** When it arrives, it starts from the same written rules the verdicts use.

---

## Try it

If you lift and you've ever wondered whether the last three months did anything, this is the app I built for that.

[**Get WhyRep on Google Play**](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.whyrep.app)

More at [whyrep.com](https://whyrep.com).

Log the same lift twice and WhyRep starts judging it. The 3-day trial shows you every verdict and the reason behind it. Then tell me the first one you disagreed with. That's the most useful feedback I can get, because it means either the rule is wrong or the explanation is.

Q&A with Al Chen, Software Engineering Leader at Cisco

We interviewed Al Chen for year's AI Engineer NYC event. Al is a Software Engineering Leader at Cisco, where he leads the customer engineering team for Splunk Agent Observability (formerly Galileo). He specializes in production AI infrastructure, enterprise deployments, and agent engineering.

We talked about what it really takes to deploy AI agents inside major banks, from navigating security reviews and compliance requirements to preventing data leaks and designing agents that fail gracefully.

Here's our conversation.

## Tell us about your talk.

The talk is a bit of war stories: our experiences deploying our platform inside various banks, how we get through the different compliance, security, and legal gates, and some of the potential solutions on the path forward. That's the main gist, and I'll walk through a few deep-dive examples.

## How did you get into this work?

My path into AI was kind of circuitous. Like many people out there, I wasn't doing this even three years ago. I come from the world of spreadsheets and productivity software. I got the AI bug in 2023, early 2024, and I was super skeptical at first. I saw ChatGPT and thought, this is great for small use cases. Then I dug in some more and got really into the weeds with LangChain and different AI frameworks. About a year ago I had the opportunity to join a small startup, Galileo, which was acquired by Cisco. We're deploying our software within the largest banks and financial institutions in the world, and that's how I ended up dealing with CVEs on an everyday basis.

## You've taken agent tooling into five Fortune 100 banks. What breaks first when a stack built for SaaS hits a tier 1 bank security review?

The first thing that breaks, and I'm going to talk about this at the conference, is dealing with CVEs: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. It's probably the number one thing all of our banks deal with. Before we even touch one piece of hardware or software, getting through that gate is the biggest hurdle. Until you have a really buttoned-down process for remediating vulnerabilities in your software, it's a showstopper for getting anything through the front door of a bank.

My team is on the frontlines of dealing with these day in, day out. It's a full-time job. Really, it's a full team's job. The problem is each bank has its own unique process, its own policies, and its own scanning software to determine what counts as an exploit or a vulnerability.

My job is to figure out how to systematize this, because we don't want to deploy bespoke solutions for every single customer. How do you do it all as one cohesive process? That's definitely been a challenge, and I'm curious to hear how others are doing it. Even at a big company like Cisco, we're probably still figuring out how to deal with different customers.

## How do you split your time day to day between execution, strategy, learning, and problem solving?

It's the typical startup phrase: you're building the plane while you're flying it. I didn't know anything about CVEs or Kubernetes clusters before this role. I'm using AI to learn about these things, but until I really grasp the concepts, I still have to do some of my own self-teaching.

GiffyPy: A Fast, Lightweight Video Editor for Your Project README

If you've ever tried adding a GIF or animated WebP of a screen recording to your project's README, you know how annoying it can be. You just want to show people how your product works without spending 20 minutes editing a video, but a few friction points always pop up.

A good README is important. Seeing an app in action builds way more trust than a wall of text. So I built **GiffyPy**, a lightweight video editor specifically designed to make editing screen recordings for project READMEs fast and effortless.

Here are the main problems it solves (or [click here](https://github.com/effessdev/GiffyPy) to skip directly to the GitHub repository).

## Removing the taskbar and black borders

When recording your screen with OBS Studio, even if you use Window Capture, you can end up with black bars or the taskbar stuck in the recording.

![obs-recording](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/60jp4mmuxzbiqvxfj2ml.png)

Cropping it cleanly in a regular video editor can involve trial and error with resolutions. GiffyPy lets you drag and resize a crop rectangle directly over the video preview, just like cropping an image.

It also includes rule-of-thirds guides to help position the crop.

## A proper multi-clip timeline

Previously, I mainly needed to trim the beginning and end of a recording. But sometimes you want to remove a few sections in the middle or rearrange parts of a demo.

GiffyPy now has a **non-destructive, multi-clip timeline** that lets you:

- Split clips at the current playhead position using `S`.
- Trim the start and end of clips by dragging their edges.
- Reorder segments using drag and drop.
- Delete unwanted segments.
- Undo the last edit using `Ctrl + Z`.

The original video stays untouched, so you can experiment with the edit without permanently modifying the source file.

## Instant scrubbing without loading screens

I usually only need to make a few quick edits, so waiting for a heavy editor to load or dealing with sluggish timeline scrubbing feels unnecessary.

GiffyPy opens in under a second. During import, it generates a low-resolution image sequence so the preview can update quickly while you scrub.

While dragging the playhead, it displays these lightweight images. Once you release the mouse, it switches back to the full-resolution frame.

It can also generate background proxy files for video codecs that Qt cannot play natively, helping expand the range of videos you can edit.

## Optimizing GIFs and videos

A screen recording doesn't need to be huge just to demonstrate a feature in a README.

GiffyPy lets you customize the export using three main settings:

- **Framerate:** Adjust the output from 0.5 to 60 FPS.
- **Resolution:** Scale the output dimensions as a percentage.
- **Quality:** Adjust the output quality to balance file size and visual clarity.

For GIF exports, it also supports automatic palette generation and dithering controls, giving you more control over the final result.

![GiffyPy export settings](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/7lc3fvo651o4zufvtm6f.png)

The goal is to keep demos lightweight while making sure they still look good.

## Faster exports and four ways to save

Exporting shouldn't interrupt your workflow with a file dialog every time.

GiffyPy now provides four separate save options:

- **Overwrite Existing File:** Replace the source file's existing output, with a confirmation prompt first.
- **Save a Numbered Copy:** Save a new version next to the source, using a name like `name (edited 1)`.
- **Save To…:** Choose the output location and filename yourself.
- **Copy to Clipboard:** Export and copy the result directly to your clipboard.

The last option is particularly useful for README demos. You can copy an animated GIF or WebP and paste it directly into places that support image pasting, such as GitHub or DEV.to's editors.

No need to export to a folder, find the file, and manually attach it afterward.

*Note: Clipboard export is currently available for GIF and WebP only.*

## Multiple export formats

Although the main goal is creating lightweight animations for project READMEs, GiffyPy isn't limited to GIFs.

It currently supports exporting to:

- Animated WebP
- GIF
- MP4
- WebM
- MOV
- MKV

So you can use it for ordinary video exports too, not just README demos.

## Timeline navigation and keyboard shortcuts

The timeline also has a few navigation controls to make editing more comfortable, especially for longer recordings.

- **Scroll** to move through the timeline.
- **Zoom** using `Ctrl + Scroll` or a two-finger trackpad gesture.
- **Pan** using middle-click and drag or a two-finger trackpad gesture.
- **Move frame by frame** using the left and right arrow keys.

There are also shortcuts for common actions, including splitting clips, deleting segments, undoing edits, and fitting the timeline to the view.

The idea is to keep the workflow fast without forcing you to reach for the mouse for every operation.

## A custom app icon

Not a big feature, but a custom icon in the taskbar matters to me!

![GiffyPy custom icon](https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/pp4flrhgew6lv3lrew03.png)

It's a small detail, but it makes the app feel more complete.

## How it was made

GiffyPy is built with **Python and PySide6**, with FFmpeg handling video processing and export.

The source code is available on GitHub:

👉 [effessdev/GiffyPy](https://github.com/effessdev/GiffyPy)

### Requirements

FFmpeg needs to be installed and available in your system's `PATH`.

On Windows, you can install it from the command prompt using:

```bash
winget install Gyan.FFmpeg
```

### Building a standalone Windows executable

GiffyPy also includes a packaging script for building a standalone Windows executable using PyInstaller.

From the project directory, run:

```cmd
package.bat
```

The script packages the app using `main.py` and includes the custom `icon.ico`.

## What's next?

GiffyPy already covers most of my personal needs for creating screen recordings for READMEs, but there's always room for improvement.

I'd love to hear what you think:

- What features would make this kind of editor more useful to you?
- Are there any annoying steps in your current screen-recording workflow that could be automated?
- Would you use a lightweight editor specifically designed for creating README demos?

If you work on open-source projects, I'd especially love to hear how you currently create and optimize your demo GIFs.

@ssapable created a cartoon for GiffyPy using a tool he built called [ScriptToon](https://payhip.com/b/A2wa8). [Click here](https://ssap-pa.github.io/scripttoon-samples/giffypy-3d.mp4) to view it; it's really good!

Give GiffyPy a try, check out the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/effessdev/GiffyPy), and let me know what you think!

8 Posts by Women on DEV That Deserve More Than a Once-a-Year Spotlight

We went looking for good posts by women on DEV. Not "inspirational," not "diverse" but just genuinely good, the kind you'd send to a friend with "okay you have to read this one" attached. Here are eight, and the honest reasons each one earns your attention.

> **A note from Mika, SheShips creator**
>
> This is the first post from SheShips, soooo hi. I'm Mika, and I started this because I kept finding great posts by women on DEV that and I wanted to bring them the attention they deserved, and I didn't see a space built specifically to change that.

## Anna Villarreal — DEV Follower Analysis

{% link https://dev.to/annavi11arrea1/dev-follower-analysis-4dhc %}

This is what a good tangent looks like. Anna was seven hours into an unrelated Node.js tutorial when the thought hit her sideways: what if she scraped her own DEV followers, pulled their public GitHub data via GraphQL, and actually looked at who was reading her stuff?

There wasn't a plug-and-play tool for this. So she built one — a scraper, a JSON export, a chart at the end. What makes the post worth reading isn't the follower-count gimmick, it's that she's honest about the process being genuinely a little annoying to figure out. "There isn't a plug-and-play solution for this, you have to be a tiny bit creative," she writes. That's the whole game, most days.

{% link https://dev.to/sizzlebop/i-built-a-local-ai-music-studio-3fb9 %}

A working answer to "why do I need a subscription and a cloud account just to mess around with AI music generation." Local-first tools like this get way less airtime than their SaaS equivalents, which is exactly why this one deserves the spotlight — someone did the less-flashy, more-useful version and wrote it up.

## sylwia-lask — What If Your AI Agent Never Had to Leave the Browser? (Demo)

{% link https://dev.to/sylwia-lask/what-if-your-ai-agent-never-had-to-leave-the-browser-demo--5g %}

Good because it's a demo, not a hot take. Half the AI-agent discourse right now is pure speculation in a thread somewhere. This one just answers the question by shipping the thing and letting you go look at it yourself.

## thesnehamk — MCP vs API Explained: Do We Still Need APIs After MCP?

{% link http://dev.to/thesnehamk/mcp-vs-api-explained-do-we-still-need-apis-after-mcp-2kkk %}

The explainer post that earns its spot by asking the question a lot of developers are quietly unsure about but don't want to say out loud in a meeting. Direct, timely, no padding.

## maame-codes — Disappeared Since March: Taking a Long Break Was My Best Decision Yet

{% link https://dev.to/maame-codes/disappeared-since-march-taking-a-long-break-was-my-best-decision-yet-1n45 %}

Not a build post, and that's exactly why it belongs on this list. Writing honestly about stepping away is harder than writing a project devlog, and rarer. If you've ever felt weird about a gap in your own output, this one's for you.

## Ava Barron — Can You Stand the Rain

{% link https://dev.to/abarron/can-you-stand-the-rain-4e0k %}

An origin story that refuses the tidy version. Her path into tech runs through an Alicia Keys concert and fixing friends' computers over AIM as a teenager — not a bootcamp, not a CS degree, not a straight line. It won DEV's own 2026 WeCoded "Echoes of Experience" category, and it earns that win through specificity — nothing in it is generic.

## Margarita — It Wasn't Brave. It Was Just Tuesday.

{% link https://dev.to/it_is_margarita/it-wasnt-brave-it-was-just-tuesday-3673 %}

Also a WeCoded winner, and what makes this one work is its refusal to dramatize. Three generations of one family, all pulled toward logic and systems, told plainly — no inflating it into a bigger moment than it actually was. The title does the whole argument by itself.

## Ashley Childress — Forged Between Coal and Code

{% link https://dev.to/anchildress1/forged-between-coal-and-code-phi %}

The most technically ambitious thing on this list. A fully narrated, self-voiced web experience about growing up in an Appalachian coal town and finding her way into engineering — backed by 685 unit tests and 220 E2E tests, for what's nominally a personal art piece. It won DEV's Frontend Art category, and honestly, the craftsmanship is doing as much work as the story is.

---

That's the list. Eight different reasons to click through, eight different kinds of good. Go read one.

---

### Building something? We want to see it.

SheShips is a space for women who build and ship real software — whatever that looks like for you. A devlog, a first open-source contribution, an experiment that didn't work, a tutorial explaining the thing you learned three days ago. If you've got something you're working on, [join us on DEV](https://dev.to/sheships) and share it. We'd love to feature you in the next one of these.

Design for Churn

The biggest design shift of the AI era isn’t about who writes the code. It’s about how long the code is expected to live.

Churn has always been a dirty word in software. Microsoft researchers [showed years ago](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-of-relative-code-churn-measures-to-predict-system-defect-density/) that relative code churn predicts defect density. Adam Tornhill wrote a whole book called [*Your Code as a Crime Scene*](https://pragprog.com/titles/atcrime2/your-code-as-a-crime-scene-second-edition/), where frequently changed, complex files are the first suspects. [GitClear’s research](https://www.gitclear.com/coding_on_copilot_data_shows_ais_downward_pressure_on_code_quality) projected that AI assistants would double the share of code rewritten within two weeks of being written, and framed that as downward pressure on quality. The instinct runs deep: code that keeps changing is code that was wrong.

But that instinct comes from a world where writing code was expensive. Durability was how you got your money’s worth. When a feature costs an afternoon instead of a sprint, the math flips. Rewriting something is often cheaper than carefully preserving it, and that’s only going to become more true.

## Codebases are gardens now

We’ve always described software in building terms: architecture, foundations, scaffolding, load-bearing walls. Buildings are supposed to stand still.

I think codebases are becoming more like gardens. Specifically, gardens full of annuals. A gardener replants annuals every season, and nobody calls a tomato plant technical debt because it dies in October. The gardener’s real investment goes into what *doesn’t* turn over: the soil, the beds, the irrigation, the oak tree in the corner. Good structure is exactly what makes replanting cheap.

Code that churns a lot is essentially disposable, and disposable doesn’t have to mean sloppy. It can still be well made. It just isn’t made to last. Quality for an annual means it does its job, it’s tested at its edges, and it can come out without tearing up everything around it.

The problem is that we don’t have a picture of what high-quality churn looks like yet. Our mental model of quality is tangled up with longevity. We brag about code that has run untouched for six years. So churn happens anyway, but implicitly, and it lands wherever is most convenient.

## Where churn actually lands

I looked at the last six months of [Forem](https://github.com/forem/forem): 563 commits. The most-churned file is `app/models/article.rb`, touched in 37 of them.

Our spam handler is up there too, at 13. That one I’m happy about. Spam is a seasonal crop. Spammers change tactics constantly, and our code should churn right along with them.

`article.rb` is the oak tree. When the oak gets dug up every week, it means new features are rooting themselves in the core model because that was the easiest place to plant them. That’s the structural compromise. Churn isn’t the problem. Unplanned churn in load-bearing places is.

## Designing for it

A few ideas for making churn explicit instead of accidental:

**Name the layers.** Say out loud what’s an annual and what’s a perennial. Our `AGENTS.md` already does a crude version of this by telling AI assistants to tread carefully around core auth, feed sorting, and cache pipelines. That should be more than a warning label. It should be the shape of the codebase.

**Put contracts at the edges of the beds.** Interfaces, schemas, API specs, and tests that pin behavior rather than implementation are the perennials. Whatever sits behind them can be rewritten freely, by a person or an agent.

**Make removal cheap.** The test of a good annual is whether you can pull it out without disturbing the bed. If something is meant to churn, it shouldn’t have tendrils in everything.

**Measure churn by layer.** High churn in the fast layer is a sign of health. Churn in the slow layer is the alarm.

## Churn is a design input

Churn is going to happen either way. AI has made it the default rate of change for most of what we build. We can keep treating it as a symptom, or we can treat it as a design input and build the structure that lets us replant with confidence.

I will acknowledge that I have always been more of the perspective that churn is more acceptable than conventional wisdom of software design has implied. I’ve never seen the avoidance of churn as being a good thing in my practical experience. I used to see both sides of the argument, now I am staunchly in the camp that churn is positively associated with the quality and rigidity of our codebases and our systems.

I’d rather tend the garden than pretend it’s a building.
